newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity front months lower, backs gain.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity front months lower, backs gain.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures front months were trading lower Friday under some pressure from natural gas prices, while summer months showed strength in anticipation of air conditioning demand, industry sources said.
As of 1200 EST, March California Oregon Border (COB) futures were trading down eight cents at $10.95 per megawatt hour (MWh) after exchanges as low as $10.85.
April COB was bid at $10.00 and offered at $10.20 from Thursday's settle price of $10.10 per MWh.
July COB was trading up 10 cents at $13.85 per MWh.
March Palo Verde (PV) was down 23 cents at $13.05 after trading in a range of $12.85-13.10, while April PV was up 10 cents at $12.20 per MWh.
As of 1210 EST, NYMEX March natural gas futures were trading down 12.6 cents at $2.235 per million British thermal units.
The Bonneville Power Administration said it was not offering peak power on Saturday and Monday, although the agency did offer electricity for heavy-load hours on Sunday.
NYMEX said that as of 1140 EST an estimated total of 13 COB and 49 PV contracts had traded.
Forecasts called for the Pacific Northwest to see temperatures from two to five degrees Fahrenheit below normal for the next several days, with some moisture in the western portions of the region.
Longer-term forecasts called for below and much below temperatures through most of the Northwest from Feb 11 to 15.
In the Southwest, forecasts called for temperatures to be three to six degrees below normal into Saturday, with some scattered light precipitation over the north and western sections.
The Southwest was expected to see near normal temperatures from Feb 11 to 15, with the exception of Arizona which was called to have above-normal temperatures.
A 1,100 megawatt (MW) pumped storage hydroelectric plant near Fresno, Calif., was shut last Saturday for mechanical repairs, and could stay down for up to two weeks.

The 1,158 MW WNP-2 nuclear power plant at Richland, Wash., was operating at 67 percent of capacity as of early Friday but will reduce power to 25 pct of capacity due to ongoing problems with an adjustble speed drive.
